llm.summary: The skill is an SQL helper, but it includes mismatched scripts, unsafe SQL text generation from unvalidated names, and undisclosed local command-history logging that users should review before installing.

dimensions.detail: sql.sh is local and does not connect to databases, but script.sh creates a user data directory and records command arguments even though that persistence is not disclosed in SKILL.md and is not necessary for the stated SQL-generation purpose.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: No privileged installer, dependency fetch, network setup, or system hook was found, but command mapping is unclear because SKILL.md tells users to run sql-generator while the package ships separate script.sh and sql.sh files.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The trigger and capability description are broad and do not set boundaries for production use, destructive SQL, DDL, migrations, or review-before-execution despite generating statements users may run against real databases.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: script.sh appends command arguments to a persistent history.log under SQL_GENERATOR_DIR or the user's local share directory without documented retention, clearing, or explicit restrictive permissions; no privilege escalation or backdoor persistence was found.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

dimensions.detail: The main purpose is SQL generation and sql.sh does generate templates, but SKILL.md advertises commands such as explain, optimize, create, mock, migrate, and cheatsheet while the actual sql.sh only exposes table, query, index, seed, and help; script.sh is an unrelated data-processing wrapper that mostly echoes status text.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

llm.guidance: Review generated SQL before running it, especially DDL, INSERT, index, migration, UPDATE, DELETE, DROP, or ALTER statements. Avoid passing sensitive SQL, customer identifiers, credentials, or private file paths to the bundled sql-generator wrapper unless you are comfortable with local history logging, and prefer staging databases, backups, transactions, and least-privileged database accounts.
llm.findings:
[SQP-1] expected: The SQL-generator activation language is purpose-related, but it is broad and lacks safety boundaries, so this supports a scoping concern rather than a malicious finding.
[SQP-2] expected: DDL, mock data, and optimization SQL are consistent with the advertised purpose, but the absence of warnings or safeguards around write/DDL output is a real review concern because users may execute the generated SQL.
[SDI-4] unexpected: The data-processing script is not coherent with the SQL-generator purpose and its import/export/transform/clean commands mostly echo text and log history, so this finding is accepted as purpose-mismatch evidence.
[SQP-3] expected: Chinese-first help text and examples match much of the package content and are mainly a localization/usability limitation, not a standalone security reason for escalation.
[SQP-3] expected: tips.md is Chinese-only instructional content; this is under-disclosed for non-Chinese users but not evidence of hidden execution, exfiltration, or privilege abuse.
[T09] unexpected: The unvalidated table-name interpolation in sql.sh can emit injected SQL if a malicious identifier is supplied and a user later executes the generated output; the script does not execute database commands itself, so this is a generated-output safety issue, not direct compromise.
[T09] unexpected: The plaintext persistent history in script.sh is not disclosed by the skill instructions and can retain SQL fragments or local paths; no network transmission or privilege escalation was found.
